meta.title: Who really said "Beam me up, Scotty"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Never spoken on screen. The closest is Kirk's 'Scotty, beam me up!' in Star Trek IV (1986) - and the catchphrase was already in print by 1975.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Beam me up, Scotty'?
meta.ogDescription: The words are real; the order isn't. Kirk says 'Scotty, beam me up!' in Star Trek IV (1986) - but the catchphrase beat the film into print by 11 years.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “Scotty, beam me up!”
answer.authorName: Steve Meerson, Peter Krikes, Harve Bennett & Nicholas Meyer
answer.authorDates: Credited screenplay team · Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (Paramount, 1986)
answer.sourceLine: The words are real, the order is not. In Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (1986), Kirk tells Gillian Taylor “Thank you, …for everything. Scotty, beam me up!” — the same four words the public quotes, simply front-loaded with the name. No Star Trek episode or film contains the sentence in its famous order, and the catchphrase was already in print in 1975, eleven years before this film gave it its closest on-screen echo.

source.heading: The line as actually filmed

docMeta.dd: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (Paramount Pictures, 1986)
Screenplay by Steve Meerson, Peter Krikes, Harve Bennett & Nicholas Meyer; story by Harve Bennett & Leonard Nimoy. Directed by Leonard Nimoy. Credit settled by WGA arbitration.
Adm. James T. Kirk (William Shatner) — a fictional character
Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, 1986; Kirk parting from Gillian Taylor

source.excerpt: Thank you, …for everything. Scotty, beam me up!
trail: The wording. Wikiquote's page for the film is a selection, not a transcript, and does not carry the line at all — so the claim was checked against the full film transcript ↗, where Kirk's Golden Gate Park line reads “Thank you, …for everything. Scotty, beam me up!” Same four words as the catchphrase; different order.

The specialist anchor. Quote Investigator has no article on this phrase, so the authority is Fred R. Shapiro of The Yale Book of Quotations ↗, who confirms the phrase was never said in the original series and dates its earliest documented appearance to the Aeronautical Journal, April 1975. This page adopts that date and asserts nothing earlier.

The negative claim. Wikipedia ↗ states the exact phrase “was never actually spoken in any Star Trek television episode or film,” and independently names Star Trek IV as carrying “Scotty, beam me up” — an attribution that page leaves uncited, which is why it was confirmed against the transcript above rather than taken on trust.

The authorship. The four-way screenplay credit, the Writers Guild arbitration that produced it, and the note that Meyer wrote the 20th-century Earth section in which this line falls all come from Wikipedia's article on the film ↗. No source assigns this particular sentence to one writer, so none is named here.
source.excerptNote: Kirk has just prised the whales' tracking frequency out of Gillian Taylor and is refusing to take her to the 23rd century; he gives the order, and she leaps into his arms and transports with him anyway. Quoted at minimum length: the film is in copyright, and the wording — not the scene — is what this page exists to establish.

sourceLink.text: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home — full film transcript

source.rightsNote: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home was first released on 26 November 1986 and is firmly in copyright — US public domain currently reaches only works published through 1930. Screenwriting is work-for-hire: the rights sit with Paramount Pictures as the studio, not with the four credited screenwriters, who are the line's authors but not its owners. The popular wording “Beam me up, Scotty” is a separate matter — a short folk phrase of no identifiable authorship, and in any case too brief to carry copyright on its own.

author.name: Steve Meerson, Peter Krikes, Harve Bennett & Nicholas Meyer
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Credited screenwriters · Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (Paramount, 1986) · credit settled by WGA arbitration
author.bio: The real line belongs to a four-way screenplay credit, and a contested one. Paramount, dissatisfied with the first script by Steve Meerson and Peter Krikes, brought in producer Harve Bennett (1930–2015) and Wrath of Khan director Nicholas Meyer (b. 1945) to rewrite it, from a story by Bennett and Leonard Nimoy, who directed. Meyer and Bennett were originally credited alone; Krikes and Meerson filed for arbitration with the Writers Guild and were awarded credit as well — a ruling that, by Meyer's account, embittered him for years. Wikipedia records that Meyer wrote the 20th-century Earth middle portion, which is where this line falls, but no source assigns the sentence itself to any one of the four, so it is the credited team's line rather than a single writer's.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Nothing here is fabricated and nobody is falsely accused — the show is the right show and Kirk is the right captain. What went wrong is narrower and stranger: the word order, and the assumption that a script produced the phrase at all.

items.why: The catchphrase is filed in memory under the 1960s show, but the sentence appears in no episode. The nearest approaches are all worded differently: Kirk says “This is the Captain. Beam me up” in “This Side of Paradise” ↗, “Scotty, beam us up fast” in “The Savage Curtain” ↗, and “Mister Scott, beam us up” in “The Cloud Minders” ↗.

items.who: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home (1986)
items.why: The film most often produced as proof does contain every word — in the wrong order. The transcript ↗ reads “Scotty, beam me up!”, the name leading rather than trailing. Cite this film for the words if you like; you cannot cite it for the sentence.

The drift outlived the man who supposedly answered it. Wikipedia ↗ records that Doohan's obituary described him as the character who “responded to the command, ‘Beam me up, Scotty’” — a command he was never actually given. Doohan then used the phrase as the title of his 1996 autobiography.

items.who: Any Star Trek script, as the source of the phrase
items.why: This is the load-bearing error. Fred Shapiro dates the wording in print to the Aeronautical Journal, April 1975 ↗ — eleven years before Star Trek IV. No screenplay can be the origin of a phrase that was already circulating before it was written.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody wrote “Beam me up, Scotty.” The closest anyone came on screen is Kirk's “Scotty, beam me up!” ↗ in Star Trek IV (1986) — and by then the catchphrase had been in print for eleven years. It is less a misquotation of Star Trek than a piece of folk language the franchise never quite caught up with.
